title: Warm pre-spawn water came with earlier Pacific herring spawning in four of five British Columbia regions in 1951-2026, but coastal warming explains less than 1 day per decade of timing trends
abstract: We tested what sets the date of Pacific herring spawning in British Columbia. We used 31,460 dated DFO spawn records (1951-2026, seven stock regions), daily lightstation sea-surface temperature (SST) and the ages of 1.3 million herring in DFO biosamples. The plan was written before we joined timing to temperature or age. Year to year, the spawn-weighted median date was earlier by 2.5-5.3 days per 1 C of mean SST in a fixed 60-day pre-spawn window in Haida Gwaii, Prince Rupert, Central Coast and Strait of Georgia (95% CIs below zero); the West Coast of Vancouver Island slope was uncertain (-1.3). The pooled slope was -3.6 days/C (95% CI -4.9 to -2.3). Other stations, windows, lags, year terms and timing quantiles kept negative slopes. Pre-spawn SST increased by only 0.10-0.15 C per decade, which implies 0.1-0.8 days per decade earlier spawning. At fixed spawn locations, timing moved later than this in the Central Coast (+1.1 days/decade beyond the SST prediction) and Strait of Georgia (+0.6), and earlier in Prince Rupert (-2.0). In the Strait of Georgia the regional median moved earlier only because spawning concentrated in an early area (Statistical Area 14). Mean spawner age had no repeated link to timing (pooled -0.3 days per year of age, 95% CI -2.1 to +1.4). Models fitted on 1951-1990 predicted 1991-2026 timing with small skill (pooled 0.105 for SST; age added nothing). Limitations: one coastal SST point per region, survey start dates and a 1988 change to dive surveys, and fishery-based age samples. The Prince Rupert advance and the later fixed-location timing elsewhere stay unexplained.
